title: Abu Bakr's first speech
hook: obey me as long as I obey Allah, and if I go wrong, set me right (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatimah: two whispers, a grave, and a daughter who followed her father soon. Your line was: she followed him soon. Did you say the thing you didn't want to leave unsaid? Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

A new leader stands up in front of the people for the first time. What does a person usually say in that moment? Something about strength. Something about a plan. Something about how things are going to be better now. Abu Bakr, the Prophet's longtime friend, has just received the pledge of the community in Medina. Sunni Muslims remember this as the moment he took office as caliph; Shia Muslims, as this week has shown, remember the succession differently. Either way, the speech the sources give him is short, and it doesn't sound like a victory speech at all. It sounds like a man asking to be watched. Today: Abu Bakr's first speech.
screen: `A NEW LEADER STANDS UP.` → `NO VICTORY SPEECH.` → `A MAN ASKING TO BE WATCHED.`

segments.voice: The speech comes to us through the sirah, the early biographies of the Prophet, in the work of Ibn Ishaq as passed on by Ibn Hisham. In paraphrase, it goes like this. I have been put in charge of you, and I am not the best of you. If I do well, help me. If I do wrong, set me right. Truthfulness is a trust, and lying is a betrayal. The weak among you is strong in my eyes until I get him his right, and the strong among you is weak in my eyes until I take from him what he owes. Obey me as long as I obey God and His Messenger, and if I disobey them, you owe me no obedience. Take it a line at a time. First, I am not the best of you. He opens by lowering himself, not raising himself. Second, set me right. He is handing the people the job of correcting him. Third, the weak and the strong. Power usually leans toward the strong. He says it will lean the other way until rights are paid. And fourth, the limit. Obedience has an edge: it stops where he stops obeying God. A leader who writes his own limit into his first words is telling the people where the line is before anyone has to find it. In Sunni teaching, this speech is read as a picture of how authority should sit on a person: lightly, and under God.
screen: `I AM NOT THE BEST OF YOU.` · `IF I DO WRONG, SET ME RIGHT.` · `THE WEAK ARE STRONG WITH ME.` · `NO OBEDIENCE IF I DISOBEY GOD.` · then, large: `SET ME RIGHT.`

segments.voice: The practice: invite correction. Sit back, and let a breath out slowly. Think of one place where you have a little authority. At work, at home, over a younger sibling, in a group chat you run. Breathe in, and ask yourself honestly: who would tell me if I were getting this wrong? Breathe out. Pick one person you trust, and decide, here in the quiet, that you'll ask them this week: is there anything I should be doing differently? Hold the question until it stops feeling dangerous. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr. The Prophet's longtime friend, who in his first speech as leader said: I am not the best of you; if I do well, help me; if I do wrong, set me right. Today's word.

Your line: set me right. Today, ask one person to tell you where you could do better, and thank them for the answer. And look back at the week: the generation, saqifah, two tellings, Ghadir Khumm, Fatimah, and a leader asking to be corrected. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Abu Bakr's first address is often quoted by Sunni Muslims in sermons and teaching about leadership, especially its lines asking the people to help him when he does well and set him right when he does wrong.

fork.setup: you've just been chosen to lead a grieving community. it's your first time speaking to them as leader. what do you say?
options: promise them you'll make everything better.
tell them you're not the best of them, and ask them to correct you.
remind them they must obey you.
fork.reveal: the sirah gives Abu Bakr the second: I am not the best of you; if I do well, help me; if I do wrong, set me right.

original.note: Arabic: 'set me right', the request at the heart of the speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: a new ruler's speech about his power.
what it means: a speech about his limits: help me, correct me, and stop obeying me if I disobey God.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq places the speech on the day after the saqifah, at the general pledge in the mosque, and its key verb is qawwimuni: set me right.
recall: the freed man of Abu Hudhayfah

sources.ref: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, from Ibn Ishaq (Abu Bakr's address after the pledge)

notes: Speech paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq / Ibn Hisham; Guillaume's English (1955) is not public domain. Confirm the paraphrase, including the line on truthfulness and betrayal.
